newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ govt, Labour at odds over GDP data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ govt, Labour at odds over GDP data.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said Treasury's upbeat growth forecasts were validated by GDP data released on Friday, just 15 days before a general election.

However, opposition Labour party finance spokesman Michael Cullen called the GDP figures "poor", pointing to slowing growth in two sectors vital to New Zealand's economic wellbeing -- manufacturing and agriculture.
Earlier, Statistics New Zealand said production-based GDP grew an actual 2.6 percent in the June year, against economists' expectations of a 2.3 percent rise.

"The 2.6 percent annual growth shown in today's results will improve public confidence in the ability of the economy to move forward successfully next year into further improved non-inflationary growth," Birch said.

Treasury's growth forecasts, released earlier this month, were higher than Reserve Bank of New Zealand and private sector forecasts. They predicted growth climbing again to 3.7 percent in 1997/98, 3.0 percent in 1998/99 and 3.5 percent in 1999/2000.

Labour's Cullen said the annual growth rate had been falling for eight quarters, and the 0.3 percent rise in production based GDP in the June quarter was the lowest quarterly rate since September 1992.
He said manufacturing activity had fallen on an annual basis in each of the past two quarters, and the farm sector had seen a decline in five of the last eight quarters.
"The fact they are in decline is a worrying signal, even to Bill Birch and his advisors, that all is not well in the New Zealand economy," Cullen said.

He said there were clear signs that the economic slowdown was impacting on jobs, and the governing National Party was going into a general election on October 12 with unemployment rising and economic activity falling.
Bancorp executive director Roger Kerr said while the data confirmed to some extent the slowdown in the economy, the election outcome would determine whether that trend was continued or reversed.

"An election result which would see no major changes to the fundamental economic direction of the country could see merry December optimism filtering through to the beginning of next year, and the resulting GDP growth pushing above 2.0 percent once again and on its way to 3.0 percent by the end of 1997.
"Conversely, the prospects of a centre-left government would see optimism plunging deeper and taking growth with it," he wrote in a commentary.
Recent opinion polls suggest a centre-left coalition is the most likely outcome of the election, New Zealand's first under a proportional voting system.

Other economists agreed the data showed a slowing economy, and said although this would please the Reserve Bank in its fight to keep underlying inflation between zero and two percent, it did not alter prospects for an easing in monetary conditions.
"(It is) still a reasonable rate of growth -- the economy is not collapsing," said ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said monetary policy would be driven more by house prices, wages, and any developments in fiscal policy after the election.
